title: The third sight: a dead man
hookLine: a funeral procession, the mourners weeping; the prince goes quiet

lines: A CROWD COMING THE OTHER WAY.
cards: Most of us remember a first funeral. The smell of the flowers. Shoes that pinched.
An adult you'd never seen cry, crying. Something in the room could not be fixed. The prince had never had that day.
Now Channa's chariot meets a crowd coming the other way, in mourning clothes, weeping, some beating their chests. On their shoulders, a bier. On the bier, a man wrapped in cloth, perfectly still.
The prince watches them pass, and for a while says nothing.

teach.b: When he asks, the question is simple. What is that? Channa says: a dead man.
He won't see his mother or father again, and they won't see him. Will I die too? Yes.
Everyone. Old age was slow. Sickness was sudden.
Death is final. In the old stories he rides home shaken, and in some tellings cries out that it's shameful to be born, if this is where birth leads. The third sight adds something.
It isn't only about my death.

teach.h: THE MOURNERS ARE HALF THE SCENE.
teach.b: The mourners are the other half of the scene. Everyone we love will go, and we will go from them. That's why it hits hardest.
A practice grows straight from this moment.
The Buddha taught five things to reflect on often, and many monasteries chant them. I'm of the nature to grow old. I'm of the nature to become sick.
I'm of the nature to die. Everything and everyone dear to me will change, and I'll be parted from them. My actions are the only thing I truly own.
The teaching points the other way: not darker, vivid.
The phone call you meant to make. The person across the kitchen table, who won't always be there.
The Pali word for death is marana, and the Buddha's teaching is that looking at it calmly is how you stop wasting the time you have.

how: In many Buddhist monasteries the five remembrances are chanted regularly, and Buddhists often reflect on death (maranasati) as a regular practice, sometimes at funerals where monks chant on impermanence.

o: the funeral rite of carrying a body through town on a bier
death, which comes to all and parts us from loved ones
a time of mourning kept for a year after a death

games.q: what's inside the third sight — tap the pairs.
p: the only thing I truly own

s: reflecting on death is meant to make Buddhists gloomy
the teaching points the other way: seeing that time is short helps you stop wasting it.
the five remembrances end with owning your actions
aging, sickness, death, parting from the dear, and then: my actions are what I truly own.
the third sight is only about the prince's own death
the mourners are half the scene: everyone we love will go.

games.q: you're the prince. a funeral procession passes, the mourners weeping. what do you do?
o: look away and tell Channa to drive faster.
fall quiet, and then ask what it is.
games.why: he goes quiet, then asks. the answer, that everyone dies and is parted from those they love, sends him home shaken.

practice: Sit quietly, and bring to mind one person you have lost, recently or long ago, or someone still living whom you lost another way.
Say their name, inside or out loud, and let a picture come: a laugh, a coat, the way they said your name. If tears or gratitude come, let them; nothing else is needed.

wordCard.voice: Marana. Death: a funeral on the road, and the prince learning it comes to everyone, and parts everyone from those they love.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: death, dying. Maranasati is the practice of mindfulness of death.

carryVoice: Your line: everyone we love will go. Let it make you gentler, not afraid. Rest well.
